newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Tax drives Portuguese abroad for used car bargains.
newsitem.headline: Tax drives Portuguese abroad for used car bargains.

text.p: Portuguese consumers are flocking to buy aging cars cheaply in low tax European countries in order to import them and take advantage of a discriminatory tax regime at home, trade officials said.
Officials of the Association of Car Trade in Portugal (ACAP) estimated that some 40,000 used cars entered the country in 1996.

The Portuguese can buy used luxury models more cheaply elsewhere in Europe than in their own heavily taxed country as secondhand prices in Portugal are among the highest in the European Union and the availability of such cars is limited.

The ACAP officials said used car imports had surged from 18,000 in 1995 and 6,000 in 1994 as consumers turned to countries with low car taxes, like Germany, Belgium and Luxembourg, to buy used models, often prestige brands such as Mercedes and BMWs.

"We are pressing the government for a more neutral tax system that does not discriminate between vehicles bought in Portugal and abroad," Helder Pedro, secretary general of ACAP, told Reuters in an interview late on Tuesday.
Portuguese new car dealers were suffering because so many car buyers were now going abroad, Pedro said.

He said the rise in used car imports in recent years had made the need to reform the car tax system in Portugal more urgent and added that the socialist government had told the ACAP it would review the tax, perhaps in time for the 1998 budget.
Portugal's car tax (IA), based on cylinder capacity, is paid on purchase and diminishes the older a car becomes. Consumers also pay Value Added Tax (VAT) on new car purchases.

A consumer who buys a car that is two to three years old receives a discount of 24 percent in the IA. The IA is reduced in stages depending on the car's age to a maximum 67 percent discount for vehicles that are more than eight years old.

The average burden of tax on new car prices in Portugal exceeded 50 percent in 1996, one of the highest in the European Union (EU), ACAP said. For example, a new car costing five million escudos ($32,000) before tax would go on sale to the public for 7.5 million ($48,000) after tax.
Tax on cars with the highest cylinder capacities exceeded 100 percent of the new car price, ACAP said.
A common practice is to buy a nine- or 10-year-old prestige marque cheaply in a low tax European country, import it to Portugal and pay IA at the lowest rate before registering it.
Portuguese consumers do not have to travel abroad to buy the car but may pay a local agent a commission to conduct the transaction on their behalf.

Antonio Cavaco, head of ACAP's economics and statistics department, said he estimated that sales of new cars, which grew 8.2 percent year-on-year to 217,913 units in 1996, would have grown by 17 percent if there had been no used car imports.

Registrations of cars in Portugal grew by 27.8 percent between August and November 1996, compared with the same period in 1995, while sales between January and November 1996 increased by just seven percent year-on-year, central bank figures showed.
The supply of aging prestige brands in Portugal is tight. A decade ago few Portuguese could afford new Mercedes or BMWs.
But the increase in used car imports to Portugal had led to an aging car stock in a country that is in other respects modernising rapidly, ACAP officials said.
"One danger is that Portugal's older cars will increase pollution levels. All new cars are obliged to use catalytic converters," Cavaco said.
